reconcile.connective: Early commentators treat 'scarlet' and 'purple' as overlapping shades of the same mock-royal garment, or as two garments worn in sequence.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the point directly, juxtaposing Matthew's scarlet robe against Mark and John's purple as an unresolved discrepancy in eyewitness detail.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "What color was Jesus's robe?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: and put on him a scarlet robe, or "a red coat", as the Persic version renders it; very likely an old coat of one of their officers. The Evangelists Mark and John say it was "purple", Mar 15:17, and so the Arabic version renders it here: whether there were two garments put upon him, the one a purple vest, and the other a scarlet robe over it; or whether scarlet was used instead of purple, is not certain …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill names the scarlet/purple discrepancy directly and offers the two live harmonizations (overlapping color-terms; two garments layered).

excerpts.excerpt_text: John and Mark make mention of a purple robe, which is also a very pleasant red.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The Geneva annotators explicitly equate 'purple' with a shade of red, addressing the scarlet/purple wording gap head-on.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats the scarlet/purple wording at all three verses directly, proposing overlapping color-terms or two garments worn in sequence — Haley's Alleged Discrepancies does not cover this passage, so Gill (already surfaced on the row) serves as the passage-specific PD defense.
